## What the index measures {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The Anthropic Economic Index (AEI) publishes how conversations with one provider's model spread across the tasks of the US O\*NET occupational database, and how each conversation divides the work: in an *automation* pattern the user hands the task over, and in an *augmentation* pattern the user works through it with the model. This paper calls the automation share *delegation*. It uses the releases from {{< var design.release.r1 >}} to {{< var design.release.r6 >}}, links tasks to occupations and occupations to the {{< var design.n_industries >}} Fama–French industries, and tests hypotheses fixed in a protocol registered as {{< var pap.tag >}} on {{< var pap.date >}}. {{< var meta.wording >}}

## Who delegates, and is it changing? (RQ1) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The first hypothesis, that delegation is lower in occupations requiring more education or paying higher wages (H1), is {{< var rq1.h1.decision_text >}}: its null is not rejected at {{< var rq1.holm.h1 >}}. Within task families the automation share differs by {{< var rq1.h1.beta_e >}} percentage points per year of education (interval {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h1.human_education_years_mean.ci_high >}}), and the wage coefficient points the opposite way from the prediction without being significant at its level. Under the pre-registered robustness row R24 r5 the H1 test falls below its level, which changes no decision. The second, that delegation rises within the same task across releases (H2), is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}}: the release-level condition fails (wild-bootstrap p = {{< var rq1.h2.p_wild >}}, level {{< var rq1.holm.h2 >}}), although the task-clustered trend is {{< var rq1.h2.beta >}} percentage points per year (interval {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_high >}}, p {{< var rq1.h2.p_cluster >}}). As context, that rise is one step between two releases, then a fall, at a change in how conversations were classified, so classifier or platform drift cannot be told apart from behaviour; the balanced comparison also leaves out {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.n_tasks >}} tasks holding {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.usage_share_pct >}} per cent of usage (descriptive). The third, that users check the model's work more where errors are costly (H3), is {{< var rq1.h3.decision_text >}}: its null is not rejected, and the estimate is {{< var rq1.h3.gamma >}} percentage points of the checking share (interval {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h3.error_cost.ci_high >}}). The fourth, that countries differ in delegation beyond the mix of tasks their users bring (H4), is {{< var rq1.h4.decision_text >}}: holding task mix fixed, the automation share differs by {{< var rq1.h4.b1 >}} percentage points per unit of the log (a hundred log points) of the Anthropic Usage Index, usage relative to working-age population (interval {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h4.log_aui.ci_high >}}). Usage and income are strongly correlated across countries, so their separate contributions are hard to tell apart, though the joint test is not.

## Could versus does (RQ2) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

RQ2 is descriptive and carries no test. Across the {{< var design.n_industries >}} industries, the rank correlation between delegation exposure and the human-rated theoretical exposure scores of Eloundou and co-authors is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.rho >}} (bootstrap interval {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}} to {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}; @fig-rq2-could-vs-does). Both measures use the same occupation-to-industry employment weights, so part of the agreement is shared occupational mix. Occupations the index does not publish are assigned zero usage by assumption, not measured as zero; dropping them instead, in the pre-registered robustness row R3, lowers the correlation most. The employment weights ({{< var vintage.oews.primary >}}) were published on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after the {{< var design.formation >}} formation date of the industry measures, as were the O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}} task links, so these are out of sample in AEI data only and not strictly real-time; the strict real-time row R32 is run for the market tests only.

## Did markets price it? (RQ3) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

At {{< var power.power_pct >}} per cent power the main test's minimum detectable effect, {{< var d11.primary_mde >}} percentage points of annualised risk-adjusted return per standard deviation of exposure, exceeds rule D11's threshold of {{< var design.plausibility_pp >}} points, confirmed with that effect in view, so the market evidence is reported as what it can and cannot yet say. For H5, that more delegation-exposed industries earned risk-adjusted returns departing from the historical pattern from {{< var design.window.start >}} to {{< var design.window.end >}}, the fixed wording reads: {{< var rq3.h5.wording >}} For H5b, that delegation exposure carries information beyond theoretical exposure, it reads: {{< var rq3.h5b.wording >}} Both decisions (H5 {{< var rq3.h5.decision_text >}}, H5b {{< var rq3.h5b.decision_text >}}) rest on employment weights published inside the return window and O\*NET links postdating formation, so these tests are out of sample in AEI data only and not strictly real-time; R32 is the strict real-time row and R1 is look-ahead.

## What this does not show {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The index records conversations on one provider's platforms, classified by an unstated method that may drift across releases; it does not sample people at work and says nothing about the prospects of any occupation. The associations are descriptive, not statements of what would follow if delegation changed. The market non-rejections do not show that exposure is unrelated to returns; their power clauses say what this short window could detect. Exploratory analyses, H6 among them, are not findings.
